{{short description|About a common point of certain circles defined by an arbitrary triangle}}
In [[Euclidean geometry]], '''Musselman's theorem''' is a property of certain [[circle (geometry)|circle]]s defined by an arbitrary [[triangle]].

[[File:Musselman theorem.svg|thumb|400px]]

Specifically, let <math>T</math> be a triangle, and <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> its [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]].  Let <math>A^*</math>, <math>B^*</math>, and <math>C^*</math> be the vertices of the [[reflection triangle]] <math>T^*</math>, obtained by mirroring each vertex of <math>T</math> across the opposite side.<ref name=grinberg/>  Let <math>O</math> be the [[circumcenter]] of <math>T</math>.  Consider the three circles <math>S_A</math>, <math>S_B</math>, and <math>S_C</math> defined by the points <math>A\,O\,A^*</math>, <math>B\,O\,B^*</math>, and <math>C\,O\,C^*</math>, respectively.  The theorem says that these three '''Musselman circles''' meet in a point <math>M</math>, that is the [[circle inversion|inverse]] with respect to the circumcenter of <math>T</math> of the [[isogonal conjugate]] or the [[nine-point center]] of <math>T</math>.<ref name=wolfram/>

The common point <math>M</math> is point <math>X_{1157}</math> in [[Kimberling center|Clark Kimberling's list]] of [[triangle center]]s.<ref name=wolfram/><ref name=kimberlingX1157/>

== History ==
The theorem was proposed as an advanced problem by [[John Rogers Musselman]] and [[René Goormaghtigh]] in 1939,<ref name=muss1939/> and a proof was presented by them in 1941.<ref name=muss1941/>  A generalization of this result was stated and proved by Goormaghtigh.<ref name=ayme/>

== Goormaghtigh’s generalization ==
The generalization of Musselman's theorem by Goormaghtigh does not mention the circles explicitly.

As before, let <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> be the vertices of a triangle <math>T</math>, and <math>O</math> its circumcenter.  Let <math>H</math> be the [[orthocenter]] of <math>T</math>, that is, the intersection of its three [[altitude (triangle)|altitude lines]].  Let <math>A'</math>, <math>B'</math>, and <math>C'</math> be three points on the segments <math>OA</math>, <math>OB</math>, and <math>OC</math>, such that <math>OA'/OA=OB'/OB=OC'/OC = t</math>.  Consider the three lines <math>L_A</math>, <math>L_B</math>, and <math>L_C</math>, perpendicular to <math>OA</math>, <math>OB</math>, and <math>OC</math> though the points  <math>A'</math>, <math>B'</math>, and <math>C'</math>, respectively. Let <math>P_A</math>, <math>P_B</math>, and <math>P_C</math> be the intersections of these perpendicular with the lines <math>BC</math>, <math>CA</math>, and <math>AB</math>, respectively.

It had been observed by [[Joseph Jean Baptiste Neuberg|Joseph Neuberg]], in 1884, that the three points <math>P_A</math>, <math>P_B</math>, and <math>P_C</math> lie on a common line <math>R</math>.<ref name=neuberg1884/>  Let <math>N</math> be the projection of the circumcenter <math>O</math> on the line <math>R</math>, and <math>N'</math> the point on <math>ON</math> such that <math>ON'/ON = t</math>.  Goormaghtigh proved that <math>N'</math> is the inverse with respect to the circumcircle of <math>T</math> of the isogonal conjugate of the point <math>Q</math> on the [[Euler line]] <math>OH</math>, such that <math>QH/QO = 2t</math>.<ref name=nguyen2005/><ref name=barbu2012/>
